data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
inflation_management: The Banco de Guatemala operates an inflation-targeting framework (4% +/- 1 point since 2005), and its record is solid but food-and-fuel sensitive. Inflation ran high before the GFC, peaking at 11.4% in 2008 on the back of the global commodity boom, then collapsed to 1.9% in 2009. Through the 2010s it stayed in the 2.4-6.2% range, breaching the ceiling in 2011 (6.2%) but never losing control. The post-COVID and 2022 commodity shocks pushed it to 6.9% in 2022, the second-highest in the series; it then eased to 2.9% in 2024 and a projected 1.6% in 2025, the lowest since 2009. The pass-through of US dollar movements and food prices remains the dominant inflation channel.
debt_management: Guatemala's defining fiscal trait is restraint: gross debt was just 20.9% of GDP in 2006 and never exceeded 31.5% (in 2020, the series high), settling at a projected 27.2% in 2025, among the lowest in Latin America. The flip side is chronic underinvestment in infrastructure, health, and security, since revenues are the region's weakest relative to GDP. COVID produced only a modest debt bump (from 26.4% in 2019 to 31.5% in 2020), and the rapid GDP rebound from $77.72bn in 2020 to $113.19bn in 2024 steadily eroded the ratio. Debt sustainability is not a concern; the real question is whether any government will build the tax base needed to fund development.

key_events.event: Global financial crisis: commodity boom drove inflation to its 11.4% peak in 2008, then the bust crushed growth and remittances.
The La Linea customs-corruption scandal broke; President Otto Perez Molina was stripped of immunity and resigned on September 2, 2015.
COVID-19: GDP held near $77.7bn with only a modest debt increase, cushioned by resilient US remittances.
Ukraine-war commodity shock pushed inflation to 6.9%; nearshoring interest in Guatemalan manufacturing picked up.
Reformist Bernardo Arevalo won the presidency and took office in January 2024, amid sustained anti-corruption pressure on institutions.
GDP reached a projected $121.11bn in 2025, nearly four times its 2006 level, with inflation falling to 1.6%.

outlook_next_decade: The base case is steady 3-4% growth on remittance, export, and nearshoring inflows, with inflation near target and debt drifting down toward 25% of GDP. Upside rests on whether the Arevalo administration can turn its reform mandate into higher tax collection and infrastructure investment; downside comes from US immigration policy hitting remittances, which are a major share of household income. Guatemala's fiscal virtue is real, but the economy has outgrown its state, and that mismatch is the decade's central risk.
caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
